segments.english: 13) We learned from the words of the Gaon that there are many books that are ascribed to the names of the great sages of Israel (falsely), for the sake of some benefit that accrues to them, and we learned also that whatever is not stated explicitly in the Mishnah and in the Gemara, and that we see is the opposite of the plain sense of the Talmud, is not a tradition, and we do not rely on it. And for this reason no decisors rule from the midrashim where they disagree with the Talmud, and even the Jerusalem Talmud we do not heed where it disagrees with the Babylonian, on which all the house of Israel rely, both for leniency and for stringency, as all this is made clear in the words of our rabbis the decisors in several places. And see below, §42, what I wrote there in the name of Rabbeinu Asher, And go and learn from what Rabbi Tam ben Yichya wrote, cited in the book Rivid ha-Zahav in the laws of Passover, and these are his words: "In our time knowledge has ceased, and the hidden matters of the Torah have been hidden from the eyes of every living thing; no man knows the order of this wisdom; and whoever holds to this, there befalls him a great share of the harm and the danger (that is to say, the harm and the danger of heresy, in that there is no share for him in the God of Israel). And concerning such things our Rabbis of blessed memory warned us, 'Do not seek what is too wondrous for you, and do not inquire into what is hidden from you.' And it is enough for us what the sages of the true tradition, agreed upon from every side, have taught us in the explanation of the Torah and its commandments. According to the tradition, from man to man, until the days of Moses; and it is called the Oral Torah, on account of which Moses went up on high and stood there forty days to learn its general principles and its particulars by the rules transmitted to him from the mouth of the Power. And with these matters we are bound to occupy ourselves, for they are our life and the length of our days, and of them not one shall we err. His one law is to put to death whoever defies their word, and whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death. But the remaining allusions in them, which the sages of Kabbalah did not exhaust in their lifetimes, although they are hidden matters of the Torah and matters of the intellect; we were not commanded concerning them. For these remained for the select few to be occupied with them, in the times that were before us, etc. And not everyone who wishes to take up the Name takes it. For these are matters that are like its furnace; they are so forever. And in our time the merit of the fathers has ended, and no one holds this wisdom justly: on the contrary, they destroy the corners of the Torah and its pillars; they shudder at the sound of the trumpeters; the blind, who pass over, do not know the way where light dwells; they grope like the blind, and weary themselves seeking the door. And where they thought to gain, suddenly they shall be broken, and there is no healing. And many of the unlearned boast, saying: 'The secret of the LORD is ours; the upper waters are our heritage, not yours, you masters of the Talmud who walk in darkness.' Their heart is not with their people; their eyes are plastered over, and there is no substance in them; they are wise to do harm to themselves. For they hold fast to what the hand of their intellect is too short to reach. And they want to climb the rungs; there is no doubt that it is in their power to reach the goal. And they bring up a potsherd in their hands to scrape with it. And they become a snare to them, etc. For there comes out from them a stumbling-block, to breach the fence of the Torah and to tear down its walls. One boasts of what he does not understand, and errs in the beginnings of the Torah and its roots, and comes to heresy. And he is distanced from the place of his desire, which is the nearness of God; it would have been better for him had he not been created, all the more so to change a midrash and to annul a halakhah." Thus far his words.

tokens.note: Printed list marker, kept as the author's own (decisions, wave 1 rulings).
The paragraph does not name the Gaon, and the English does not identify him.
The Hebrew is קבלה, the word for Kabbalah. The author claims it for the Mishnah and Talmud, and here he denies that a teaching outside them is a tradition.
The Hebrew is Rabbeinu Asher, the Rosh.
ר"ת is expanded as 'Rabbi Tam', the shorter reading. 'Rabbeinu Tam' is the other expansion, given in apparatus.
Rivid ha-Zahav: 'the golden chain'. The title is transliterated; rivid is a chain or necklace.
ר"ל: 'that is to say' (רוצה לומר).
רז"ל: 'our Rabbis of blessed memory'.
קבלה with האמתית: 'the true tradition' (owner's default, Q5), with the word Kabbalah in the Hebrew.
ע"פ: 'according to' (על פי).
שבע"פ: 'of the mouth'; the Oral Torah.
The Hebrew is אשר בגללה, literally 'which on account of it'.
The Hebrew word is מדות, literally 'measures'. Here it is the rules transmitted to Moses.
הגבורה is 'the Power', a name of God (decisions).
וא' is ואחד, 'and one'; it is read with מהם and the negative in 205.
אחת דתו is a set phrase, literally 'his one law'; the English keeps it.
Literally 'their mouth'; here it means what they say.
כבשונו is literally 'like its furnace'. The paragraph does not explain the figure, and the English keeps it.
מחצצים: 'trumpeters' (blowers of a trumpet). The sense of this clause is uncertain; the English keeps the words as read.
העברים: 'those who pass over', literally 'the passers'.
The Hebrew is עמי הארץ, 'the unlearned' (decisions).
טח: 'plastered over' (Isa 44:18, see apparatus).
Literally 'the hand of their intellect is short'.
The clause reads as affirmative. The irony lies in the next clause (the potsherd, Job 2:8), and the English keeps the words without adding any.
אלהים: 'God' (decisions).

grammar: The paragraph is the author's own argument in its first half. From וז"ל (3:13.102) to עכ"ל (3:13.393) the words are Rabbi Tam's, as cited in Rivid ha-Zahav, and the quotation is marked in double quotation marks.
ולא סמכינן עליה (3:13.37-39): סמכינן is the Talmudic Aramaic first-person plural of 'to rely', and the English gives it as the plain 'we do not rely on it'.
The subject of יתפלצון (3:13.281) is not marked. The English takes the destroyers of the Torah's corners as its subject; a reader may take the blind as the subject instead.
The speech of the unlearned (3:13.307-320) has no introductory formula beyond באמרם. It is marked as direct speech inside the quotation, in single quotation marks.
אין ספק בידם להגיע (3:13.342-345) reads as an affirmative. The irony is carried by the next clause, the potsherd of 3:13.349-352.
segments.note: Paragraph 13 of the book's third chapter. The opening 'we learned' frame is the author's; the central quotation is Rabbi Tam's, and it closes with the author's 'Thus far his words'.
apparatus: Base text: Wikisource, as translated for the unit under Q2 (the 1931 scan is not yet collated for this paragraph).
ר"ת (3:13.93): 'Rabbeinu Tam' is the other expansion; 'Rabbi Tam' is kept as the shorter.
Isa 44:18: טח מראות עיניהם (their eyes plastered over).
Job 38:19: אי זה הדרך ישכן אור; the author writes דרך ישכן אור.
Isa 59:10: ימששו כעורים (they grope like the blind).
Ps 25:14: סוד ה' ליראיו; the author writes סוד ה' לנו.
Prov 6:15: פתע יבוא ... ישבר ואין מרפא; the author writes פתע ישברו ואין מרפא.
Isa 59:1: הנה לא קצרה יד ה'; echoed in קצרה יד שכלם (3:13.336-338).
Job 2:8: ויקח לו חרש להתגרד בו; echoed in חרס בידם להתגרד בו (3:13.349-351).
Jer 4:22: חכמים המה להרע; echoed in חכמים להרע לנפשם (3:13.330-332).
